storyboard.addedInformation: The strike makes the negation visible: adaptation is shown as ordinary talking, not a mask.
storyboard.claim: Adapting your style to a Red or Blue is not faking who you are.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same person saying the same thing two ways — one to a Red, one to a Blue; the message is re-packaged, not faked.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the Tokyo-bakery translation analogy: same idea, applied to Reds and Blues.

storyboard.addedInformation: The parcel literalizes 'package': the words stay the same, only the wrapping changes.
storyboard.claim: Adaptation is respect: the same message-package, repackaged for the listener.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman holding a wrapped parcel — the same package being sent with care.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From denying fakery to the positive reframe: respect plus the package metaphor.

storyboard.addedInformation: The relabeled note shows the work: same content, rewritten address label.
storyboard.claim: You write the shipping label in the recipient's language; communication happens on the listener's terms.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman holding a note parcel with a rewritten address label, offering it forward.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the package metaphor: from the parcel itself to writing its label.

storyboard.addedInformation: The blank face shows the failed result: talking happened, nothing landed.
storyboard.claim: If they didn't understand, you didn't communicate — you just made noise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman talking to empty air with a blank, uncomprehending stare back at him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The consequence of the label rule: unread label means no delivery.

storyboard.addedInformation: Signals a topic pivot: the host turns to face an uncomfortable subject head-on.
storyboard.claim: Before landing, the show must face its counterpoint: the book's massive backlash.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Erikson turning to address the camera directly, raising the uncomfortable objection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Hard pivot from the translation payoff to the critique section.

storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the disputed object on screen: the grid is what the scientists attack.
storyboard.claim: The scientific community's necessary critique targets the four-color system.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Four-Color Grid displayed while Erikson points to it as the thing under fire.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the critics from the previous beat and shows the object they criticize.

storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the book restates 'DISC assessment'; the callout carries the Marston lineage.
storyboard.claim: The four-color system is a repackaged DISC assessment tracing to Marston in the 1920s.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Erikson holding up the old DISC book — the ancestor behind the color grid.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the critique in general to its specific charge: repackaged DISC.

storyboard.addedInformation: The thinking pose stages scholarly doubt: the evidence does not hold firm.
storyboard.claim: The peer-reviewed science behind DISC is notoriously soft.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Erikson pausing in thought, weighing thin evidence that will not firm up.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the DISC charge: from its age to its softness.

storyboard.addedInformation: The self-filled questionnaire literalizes the method flaw: the data is self-reported.
storyboard.claim: Unlike gravity or the genome, DISC relies on subjective self-reporting.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman filling in his own questionnaire form — the soft instrument itself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From 'soft' in the abstract to the concrete reason: self-report forms.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slumped worried posture shows a person about to be harmed by labeling, not theory.
storyboard.claim: Beyond academic squabbles sits a real, dangerous human cost.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman slumped with quiet worry — someone about to be labeled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from academic softness to the human danger the labels create.

storyboard.addedInformation: The angry boss embodies the excused behavior: the abuse is visible, the label does the excusing.
storyboard.claim: Weaponized labels excuse toxic behavior — heard in HR departments all the time.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Stuart barking angrily at his staff while the callout names what the label excuses.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First weaponization exhibit: the abusive boss excused by his color.

storyboard.addedInformation: Boxes the quoted HR excuse so the muted viewer reads it as cited speech, not fact.
storyboard.claim: 'He's just a high Red' — the label used to demand everyone toughen up and endure him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Stuart mid-rant, the boxed excuse-label stamped beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the Dave exhibit: the exact excusing sentence.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slumped sidelined posture shows the career cost: boxed out of leadership.
storyboard.claim: 'She's just a Green' — the label used to block Sarah's promotion and box people in.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A Green passed over while the Red writes her off with the label — the box that blocks the promotion.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second weaponization exhibit: from excusing the abuser to sidelining the Green.

storyboard.addedInformation: The chains literalize 'traps them': profiling locks people into fixed boxes.
storyboard.claim: That trapping is the dark side: any tool becomes a weapon in amateur or manipulative hands.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Binding chains — the profile as a trap locking the person in.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Verdict on both exhibits: excusing Reds and boxing Greens are one dark side.

storyboard.addedInformation: The explainer's contrast gesture stages tool versus user: same blade, different hands.
storyboard.claim: A scalpel saves in a surgeon's hands and harms in a child's — and humans exceed any quadrant.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Erikson laying out the contrast: skilled hands that heal versus a child holding the same blade.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the weapon verdict to its governing analogy: the scalpel.

storyboard.addedInformation: The grid on screen is the thing declared too small: no life fits inside a swatch.
storyboard.claim: Humans are more complex than a four-quadrant graphic; no color swatch captures a life.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Four-Color Grid with Erikson gesturing past its edges — the person overflows it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the scalpel analogy: Erikson concedes the grid cannot hold a whole person.

storyboard.addedInformation: The deliberating pose stages the pragmatic question: keep the blunt tool or not.
storyboard.claim: Despite bluntness and weapon risk, does the tool still earn its keep?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Erikson pausing to weigh the blunt tool's worth against its risks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From conceding the flaws to asking the pragmatic question anyway.

storyboard.addedInformation: The screaming boss is the alternative on screen: this is the default without the frame.
storyboard.claim: Without the framework, the default is Stuart screaming at everyone on the factory floor.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Stuart red-faced and shouting across the factory floor at his people.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the keep-question with the alternative: the untranslated default.

storyboard.addedInformation: The angry pointing boss shows egocentrism in action: difference read as defect.
storyboard.claim: The default is aggressive egocentrism: without translation, different reads as defective.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Stuart jabbing his finger at anyone operating differently — defective, not diverse.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the screaming default: egocentrism that mistakes diversity for defect.

storyboard.addedInformation: The grid beside the struck insult shows the exit: the frame replaces the slur.
storyboard.claim: We default to 'idiot' — the grid forces us out of our neurological narcissism.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Four-Color Grid beside the struck insult: the frame that breaks the default.
storyboard.onScreenText: View them as an idiot (struck through)
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From naming egocentrism to the tool that breaks it: the grid.

storyboard.addedInformation: The pausing observer stages the forced pause: stopping to grant others validity.
storyboard.claim: The grid forces a pause: others operate on entirely valid terms.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman pausing mid-reaction to really look at the other person.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Unpacks how the grid breaks narcissism: first the pause.

storyboard.addedInformation: Genuine warmth shows engineered empathy landing: different hardware, understood.
storyboard.claim: Different internal hardware, highly functional — understanding it engineers empathy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman warming with real understanding toward a differently-wired colleague.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the pause: valid plus functional hardware becomes empathy.

storyboard.addedInformation: The host's summing gesture marks synthesis: everything collapses into one payoff.
storyboard.claim: The synthesis arrives: the final payoff and its opening provocation return.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Erikson gathering the threads together for the closing synthesis.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the empathy mechanism to the closing synthesis.

storyboard.addedInformation: The mistuned phone literalizes broadcasting on the wrong frequency.
storyboard.claim: Feeling surrounded by idiots means broadcasting on the wrong frequency.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman holding a phone tuned to static — the message sent, the frequency wrong.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The opening provocation restated as a broadcast problem.

storyboard.addedInformation: A single calm figure with the slur struck out: no crowd, no idiots.
storyboard.claim: The ultimate realization: you are never actually surrounded by idiots.
storyboard.concreteVisual: One calm Everyman alone in the office; the 'surrounded' slur crossed out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The payoff lands: the title insult itself is crossed out.

storyboard.addedInformation: The grid behind the barking boss translates him: Red, not idiot.
storyboard.claim: You were surrounded by untranslated colors — the barking boss is tomorrow's test.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Four-Color Grid behind Stuart barking orders without context.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Replaces the slur with the true picture: colors awaiting translation.

storyboard.addedInformation: The gleeful talker beside the drained listener stages two difficult types at once.
storyboard.claim: The derailing friend, the decimal-paralyzer, the partner who goes silent to avoid a fight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Marita happily derailing the chat while Everyman withdraws into strained silence.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues tomorrow's lineup: from the barking boss to the talker and the silent partner.

storyboard.addedInformation: The arrested gesture with the slur struck out stages the erased reflex.
storyboard.claim: Stop the reflex: never ask 'why are they so stupid' — erase that inner question.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman catching himself mid-reaction, the insult crossed out of his head.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From meeting the difficult types to killing the default reaction to them.

storyboard.addedInformation: The studying gaze on the grid shows the replacement question in action.
storyboard.claim: Instead ask what color they are hearing — take on translation and friction dissolves.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman studying the Four-Color Grid, reading the other's pace and focus.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The replacement for the erased insult: the translator's question.

storyboard.addedInformation: The clearing gaze stages friction dissolving: the conflict stays, the 'idiots' go.
storyboard.claim: When you translate, the idiots disappear — clearer than any X-ray wish.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman looking steadily at a conflict that now reads clearly, wished-for X-ray unneeded.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The reward for the translator's question: disappearance.

storyboard.addedInformation: The sliding scale replaces either-or judgment with a readable range.
storyboard.claim: Behavior is not binary but a spectrum — learn to read it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A behavior spectrum scale sliding from Binary to Spectrum.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The closing image: everything reduces to one readable spectrum.
